theysay.say: Jews don't believe in Jesus — that's basically the one thing all Jews agree on.
theysay.quick: Modern consensus, yes — but the first generation of Jesus-followers was entirely Jewish, arguing from Tanakh in synagogues. The question was born inside Judaism, not imported into it.

theysay.say: The Messiah brings world peace. Look around — did he come?
theysay.quick: That's one of the Tanakh's two portraits. The other is a king 'lowly, riding on a donkey' who is 'pierced' and mourned. The rabbis felt the tension so sharply they posited two Messiahs.

theysay.say: Isaiah 53 is about Israel, not Jesus. Read chapter 41 — the servant is named Israel.
theysay.quick: The national reading is real — but Targum Jonathan opens the passage 'my servant the Messiah,' Sanhedrin 98b names Messiah from 53:4, and 53:8 says the servant is stricken 'for the transgression of my people' — someone distinct from the people.

theysay.say: Christians mistranslate our scriptures. Almah means young woman, not virgin.
theysay.quick: Concede it: almah is 'young woman'; betulah is the technical term. But the pre-Christian Jewish translators of the Septuagint chose parthenos — 'virgin' — centuries before Matthew was born.

theysay.say: God is not a man — Numbers 23:19. That ends the conversation.
theysay.quick: In context it means God doesn't lie or waver. The Tanakh itself shows YHWH appearing in human form — eating with Abraham (Gen 18), wrestling Jacob (Gen 32) — and in Zechariah 12:10 YHWH says 'they will look on ME whom they pierced.'

theysay.say: We don't need a middleman. We repent directly to God.
theysay.quick: The Torah's own system was all mediation — priests, altar, blood, Yom Kippur. Leviticus 17:11 says God gave blood to make atonement. The real question is what replaced that in 70 CE, and on whose authority.

theysay.say: For a Jew, Christianity is idolatry. Worshiping a man is the one unforgivable line.
theysay.quick: If Yeshua is merely a man, agreed — full stop. The dispute isn't whether idolatry is evil; it's whether the pierced one of Zechariah 12:10, whom YHWH calls 'me,' is a second god or the God of Israel come near.

theysay.say: After the Holocaust, how can you possibly ask Jews to convert?
theysay.quick: No glib answer exists. Own the history first, unprompted. Then gently separate baptized Europe's crimes from a first-century Jewish claim made by Jews, from Jewish scripture, before Christendom existed to sin.

theysay.say: My family would sit shiva for me. You're asking me to die to my people.
theysay.quick: Take it at face value — the cost is real, even where the practice has softened. Never minimize it. The counter-claim isn't 'leave your people'; it's that following Israel's Messiah is the most Jewish thing a Jew can do.

theysay.say: Jesus didn't fulfill the prophecies — no third temple, no ingathering, no peace.
theysay.quick: Those belong to the reigning-king portrait, still outstanding — Christians agree. But the suffering portrait (Zech 9:9, 12:10; Isa 53; Ps 22) plus Daniel 9's timestamp had a deadline before 70 CE. Two portraits, one Messiah, two acts.

theysay.say: The virgin birth is recycled paganism — gods impregnating women.
theysay.quick: The pagan stories are lust narratives with demigod offspring. Isaiah's sign and Matthew's account have no divine consort and arise in the most anti-pagan milieu in antiquity. And the LXX's parthenos is a Jewish reading, pre-Christian.

theysay.say: You can't use the New Testament to prove the New Testament.
theysay.quick: Agreed — so don't. The case runs on Tanakh alone: Isaiah 53, Daniel 9, Zechariah 9 and 12, Psalm 22, Genesis 49. The NT then enters as first-century Jewish testimony to be tested against those texts, not as the premise.

theysay.say: You quote our Talmud when it suits you — Yoma 39b is aggadah, not history.
theysay.quick: Fair hit. Hold it loosely: not proof, but the tradition's own memory that the Yom Kippur signs went dark for the final forty years before the destruction — starting, on its own math, around 30 CE.

theysay.say: Genesis 49:10 is deathbed poetry, not a messianic countdown.
theysay.quick: Targum Onkelos didn't think so — it renders 'until Shiloh comes' as 'until Messiah comes, to whom the kingdom belongs.' The question isn't a stopwatch; it's where Judah's scepter-story was heading, and when it bent.

theysay.say: Jeremiah's new covenant is the same Torah with a new heart — nothing about a new mediator.
theysay.quick: Torah internalized, yes — but Jeremiah says 'NOT like the covenant I made with their fathers' (31:32), and it ends in forgiveness so final that sin is 'remembered no more.' New in kind, and the mechanism question hangs over verse 34.

theysay.say: Psalm 22 says 'like a lion,' not 'they pierced' — Christians doctored the text.
theysay.quick: The Masoretic Text reads ka'ari ('like a lion' — which leaves the clause verbless). The Nahal Hever scroll appears to read ka'aru ('they dug/pierced') and the pre-Christian Septuagint already read a verb. Genuinely contested — say so — and the psalm's crucifixion-shaped picture stands on far more than one word.

lessons.what: Before any verse, name what 'Christian' has meant to Jewish families — unprompted: the Rhineland massacres of 1096, the blood libel born at Norwich in 1144, expulsions from England (1290) and Spain (1492), forced disputations and Talmud burnings, Luther's 1543 'On the Jews and Their Lies,' and a Holocaust incubated in baptized Europe. Carry this history so they never have to explain it to you. Nothing else you say will land until this is on the table honestly.
lessons.ask: What has the word 'Christian' meant in your family's story?

lessons.what: Move the conversation onto ground you both accept: the Tanakh, in their canon and their categories — Torah, Nevi'im, Ketuvim; Mashiach ben David; teshuvah; olam haba. No New Testament on the table yet, no proof-texting — whole chapters, read together. A Christian who has actually read Torah (even the weekly parashah) changes the entire register of the conversation.
lessons.ask: Would you study the Prophets with me — just the Tanakh, nothing of mine on the table?

lessons.what: The Tanakh draws the Messiah twice: a reigning son of David with the nations at peace (Isa 2, 11; Dan 7) — and a figure lowly on a donkey (Zech 9:9), pierced and mourned like an only son (Zech 12:10), despised, rejected, and crushed (Isa 53; Ps 22). The rabbis saw both portraits too: their solution was two Messiahs — ben Joseph who dies in battle (Sukkah 52a, citing Zech 12:10) and ben David who reigns. The Christian claim is simpler arithmetic: one Messiah, two acts.
lessons.ask: What in the text forced the rabbis to invent a Messiah who dies?

lessons.what: Daniel 9:26 puts an anointed one 'cut off' BEFORE the people of a coming prince destroy the city and the sanctuary — before 70 CE. Genesis 49:10 keeps the scepter in Judah 'until Shiloh comes,' which Targum Onkelos reads as Messiah. And Yoma 39b preserves the tradition's own memory that for the final forty years before the destruction — from about 30 CE — the Yom Kippur lot stopped coming up in the right hand and the crimson thread stopped turning white. Whoever the Messiah is, the window the shared text draws is behind us.
lessons.ask: If an anointed one had to be cut off before the Second Temple fell — who was it?

lessons.what: Leviticus 17:11 is God's own stated mechanism: 'the life of the flesh is in the blood, and I have given it to you on the altar to make atonement for your souls.' Yom Kippur was the system's heart. Since 70 CE, rabbinic Judaism has substituted repentance, prayer, and tzedakah (Hosea 14:2; Yohanan ben Zakkai in Avot d'Rabbi Natan 4) — a pastoral answer given in catastrophe, but one the Torah itself is never recorded giving. Ask it as an honest question, not a gotcha; this is the ache Yom Kippur itself carries.
lessons.ask: On Yom Kippur, what carries your sins now — and where does the Torah say that suffices?

lessons.what: The famous move: read Isaiah 52:13–53:12 aloud together without saying where it's from, and let them tell you it sounds like the New Testament — then show them it's Isaiah, from their own scroll, centuries before Yeshua. Then one invitation, transparent about what you're asking: read the Gospel of Matthew — the most Jewish of the four, opening with a toledot from Abraham, structured around Torah, fluent in fulfillment. Not a scalp. An open book, one chapter a week, and they hold you accountable to their text.
lessons.ask: Read Matthew with me as a Jewish book — one chapter a week, and you keep me honest?

proofs.they: 'God is not a man, that he should lie' — 'I am God and not a man, the Holy One in your midst.' The incarnation is flatly excluded: whatever God is, he is not a man, and no Jew may believe otherwise.
proofs.you: Both verses are about God's character — he doesn't lie, waver, or rage like men do — not about what God is unable to do. The Tanakh itself shows YHWH appearing as a man: he eats with Abraham at Mamre (Gen 18), wrestles Jacob who says 'I have seen God face to face' (Gen 32), and sends the angel in whom 'my Name is' (Ex 23:21). The claim was never that a man became God — it's that the God of Israel entered his own creation, which Hosea's 'in your midst' sits closer to than you'd expect.

proofs.they: 'Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one.' The Shema is Judaism's heartbeat, and the Trinity breaks it. Three persons is three gods with extra steps — Maimonides made absolute, indivisible unity a principle of the faith.
proofs.you: Christians affirm the Shema — Yeshua himself quoted it verbatim as the greatest commandment (Mark 12:29). Echad can name a composite unity ('one flesh,' Gen 2:24; 'one cluster,' Num 13:23), though that alone proves nothing. What the Tanakh does carry are unresolved seams — 'let us make man' (Gen 1:26), 'the Lord GOD has sent me, and his Spirit' (Isa 48:16), 'what is his name, and what is his son's name?' (Prov 30:4). Not proofs — concede that — but cracks in the claim that the text is unitarian by definition. Trinity is a claim about the inner life of the one YHWH, not a roster of gods.

proofs.they: 'The soul who sins shall die. The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father.' 'Each shall be put to death for his own sin.' Vicarious atonement — an innocent dying for the guilty — is anti-Torah on its face.
proofs.you: Ezekiel 18 answers a proverb about inherited guilt ('the fathers ate sour grapes...'), and Deut 24:16 governs human courts — neither repeals the sacrificial system, which is voluntary substitution from end to end: hands pressed on the scapegoat's head, 'and the goat shall bear all their iniquities' (Lev 16:22); blood given by God 'to make atonement for your souls' (Lev 17:11). The line the Torah draws is between punishing an unwilling bystander and accepting a willing offering. Isaiah 53:10 puts the servant on the offering side: his soul is made an asham — a guilt offering — and he 'poured out his soul to death' himself.

proofs.they: 'I, I am the LORD, and besides me there is no savior.' Salvation belongs to God alone. Trusting a man named Jesus for salvation is, by this verse, idolatry by definition.
proofs.you: Total agreement: no one but YHWH saves. That is precisely the Christian claim — Yeshua's name means 'YHWH saves,' and the NT applies Isaiah's own exclusive language ('to me every knee shall bow,' Isa 45:23) to him not as a second deity but as YHWH's own arm revealed (Isa 53:1). Either that identification is true, or Christianity is idolatry — this verse doesn't settle the question; it frames it exactly right. The dispute was never whether God alone saves, but whether God did it himself, in person.

proofs.they: The prophet who works real signs and then says 'let us go after other gods' must be rejected — miracles included. This is the Torah's standing verdict on Jesus: whatever he did, worship of him leads Israel after a god our fathers did not know.
proofs.you: Honor the test — it's the right one. But its hinge is 'gods your fathers have not known,' and that's the entire dispute: Yeshua's first followers were Shema-praying, temple-attending Jews who claimed he was the God of Abraham's own arm, not a new god. Deut 13 rightly condemns every paganized Christ Christendom ever built; what it can't do is adjudicate the identity question by itself. Deut 18:15-19's true-prophet test — the prophet like Moses whom Israel must hear — has to be run alongside it.

proofs.they: 'Put not your trust in princes, in a son of man, in whom there is no salvation.' The psalmist could not be clearer: staking your soul on any human being — any son of man — is exactly what our scriptures forbid.
proofs.you: Read the next verse: 'his breath departs, he returns to the earth; on that very day his plans perish.' The warning is against trusting what dies and stays dead — mortal power. The Christian claim is resurrection: a Messiah whose death did not hold him (Ps 16:10, 'you will not abandon my soul to Sheol'). And the Tanakh itself presents one 'like a son of man' coming with the clouds who receives everlasting dominion and the service of all peoples (Dan 7:13-14) — and a king in Psalm 2 whom the nations are told to serve, though the 'kiss the son' reading there is text-critically contested and shouldn't be leaned on alone.

didyouknow.t: The Targum calls Isaiah's servant 'the Messiah'
didyouknow.d: Targum Jonathan (the ancient Aramaic rendering of the Prophets) opens the passage: 'Behold, my servant the Messiah shall prosper.' But it then reroutes all the suffering onto Israel and the nations, leaving the Messiah only triumph — evidence both that the messianic reading is ancient and that the suffering made its readers flinch.

didyouknow.t: The Talmud's Messiah sits among the lepers
didyouknow.d: In Sanhedrin 98a, Elijah tells Rabbi Joshua ben Levi that the Messiah is already here — sitting among the suffering poor at the gates of Rome, untying and retying his bandages one at a time so that he's ready the instant he is summoned.

didyouknow.t: One rabbinic name for Messiah: 'the leper scholar'
didyouknow.d: Sanhedrin 98b records sages deriving the Messiah's name from Isaiah 53:4 — 'surely he has borne our sicknesses... yet we esteemed him stricken' — applying the suffering-servant text directly to the Messiah.

The Talmud reports that for the last forty years before the Temple's destruction in 70 CE — that is, from about 30 CE — the Yom Kippur lot stopped coming up in the right hand, the crimson thread stopped turning white, the westernmost lamp went out, and the Temple doors opened by themselves.

Facing texts where Messiah both dies and reigns, the Talmud posits Messiah ben Joseph, who is killed in battle — with Zechariah 12:10's mourning for the pierced one applied to him — followed by Messiah ben David, who reigns. Two Messiahs, or one Messiah in two acts: that's the whole debate in miniature.

didyouknow.t: Daily messianic expectation is a Jewish principle of faith
didyouknow.d: Maimonides' twelfth principle: 'I believe with perfect faith in the coming of the Messiah; and though he tarry, I will wait daily for his coming.' Awaiting a personal Messiah is not a Christian import — it's codified rabbinic doctrine sung in the Ani Ma'amin.
didyouknow.src: Rambam, commentary on Mishnah Sanhedrin ch. 10 (Perek Chelek)

didyouknow.t: Barcelona, 1263: why 'let's study together' can sound like a trap
didyouknow.d: Nachmanides (Ramban) was compelled to debate the convert Pablo Christiani before King James I of Aragon. He argued brilliantly — including that aggadic passages aren't binding — was rewarded by the king, and still had to leave Aragon under church pressure. Coerced disputations are part of why Jewish friends may hear a Bible-study invitation as an ambush.
didyouknow.src: Vikuach ha-Ramban; records of the Disputation of Barcelona, 1263

didyouknow.t: The Aleppo Codex is a shared treasure
didyouknow.d: The crown jewel of the Masoretic text (~930 CE, vocalized by Aaron ben Asher's tradition) was damaged in the 1947 Aleppo riots — most of its Torah is still missing. Together with the Leningrad Codex (1008 CE) it anchors the Hebrew Bible that Jews and Christians both read.

didyouknow.t: Isaiah 53 was in the ground before the debate began
didyouknow.d: The Great Isaiah Scroll from Qumran (1QIsaᵃ, ~125 BCE) contains the whole book, a millennium older than the medieval codices — and substantially the same text, chapter 53 included. Nobody edited the servant in later.
didyouknow.src: 1QIsaᵃ, Shrine of the Book, Israel Museum

didyouknow.t: The Messianic Jewish movement is small but real
didyouknow.d: Commonly cited estimates — all contested — run roughly 175,000–250,000 Messianic Jews in the US across ~350–400 congregations, and about 15,000 (claims range to 30,000) in Israel in 130+ congregations. Counter-missionary organizations dispute the definitions and the counts; treat every figure as an estimate.
didyouknow.src: Israel Today / One for Israel surveys; disputed by Jews for Judaism

didyouknow.d: A persistent (and admittedly anecdotal) street-interview phenomenon: Hebrew speakers handed Isaiah 53 without a citation routinely guess it comes from the New Testament. No translation argument needed — the chapter does its own work in the original.
didyouknow.src: e.g. One for Israel street-interview projects (anecdotal)

didyouknow.t: Jewish believers you may already be quoting
didyouknow.d: Alfred Edersheim, the Vienna-born Jewish convert, wrote the classic 'Life and Times of Jesus the Messiah.' Joseph Rabinowitz founded the 'Israelites of the New Covenant' in 1880s Kishinev — widely counted the first modern Messianic congregation, decades before 'Jews for Jesus' existed.
didyouknow.src: Edersheim biographies; Kai Kjær-Hansen's research on Rabinowitz

didyouknow.t: Sitting shiva for converts — real, and softening
didyouknow.d: Mourning a family member who accepted Jesus as though they had died was genuine traditional practice. In much of the modern community it has softened into grief, anger, and distance rather than formal shiva — but the fear your friend voices is not rhetorical.
didyouknow.src: Responsa literature; contemporary Jewish communal discussion

didyouknow.t: Chabad has its own Messiah debate
didyouknow.d: Many Lubavitcher Hasidim regarded the Rebbe, Menachem Mendel Schneerson, as the presumptive Messiah; after his death in 1994 a meshichist wing continued — some still do. Orthodox critic David Berger wrote a whole book protesting that a posthumous Messiah candidacy had become tolerable inside Orthodoxy. Relevant, gently: the concept of a Messiah whose career death doesn't terminate is not unthinkable in Jewish terms.
didyouknow.src: David Berger, 'The Rebbe, the Messiah, and the Scandal of Orthodox Indifference' (2001)

didyouknow.d: The Masoretes counted letters and marked the exact middle of books to keep the Hebrew Bible stable; the Greek New Testament survives in roughly 5,800 catalogued manuscripts — the two best-attested textual traditions of antiquity. Both faiths stand on scribes who counted.
didyouknow.src: Masoretic apparatus; INTF (Münster) Greek NT manuscript catalogue

week.d: Friday sundown to Saturday nightfall: candles, kiddush, family table; for the observant, no 'work' across 39 defined categories — driving, writing, and phones included at the Orthodox end.
week.tip: Never schedule anything for Friday night or Saturday without asking. 'Shabbat shalom' on a Friday is always right.

week.d: No pork or shellfish, meat and dairy separated, certification symbols on packaging — with observance ranging from strict to 'kosher-style' to none at all.
week.tip: Ask 'do you keep kosher, and how strictly?' before hosting. A certified restaurant or sealed kosher food honors them more than your best home cooking.

week.d: Rosh Hashanah opens ten Days of Awe that close with Yom Kippur: a 25-hour fast, confession, and the liturgy's raw question of who will live and who will die — atonement sought, since 70 CE, without a temple or blood.
week.tip: Yom Kippur's ache is the open door — but never exploit it in the moment. Be a friend during the fast; have the conversation another day.

week.d: The seder is the year's great table liturgy — exodus retold, questions scripted, matzah for a week. Being invited to a seder is an honor, not a courtesy.
week.tip: Accept the invitation and read the Haggadah beforehand. Watch the afikoman: matzah broken, wrapped, hidden, and brought back — and ask your host what it means.

week.d: Orthodox (Haredi to Modern), Conservative, Reform, Reconstructionist — and a large secular/cultural majority among American Jews for whom Jewishness is peoplehood more than belief.
week.tip: Never assume observance or theology. Many proudly Jewish friends are functionally agnostic. ASK what Judaism means to them — the answer is the map.

week.d: At 13 (12 for girls in many communities) a child becomes accountable to the commandments, marked by reading Torah publicly — years of preparation for one morning.
week.tip: If invited, go. Wear the kippah offered at the door. Gifts traditionally come in multiples of 18 — chai, 'life.'

week.d: Deuteronomy 6:4-9 taken literally: the Shema handwritten on parchment fixed to the doorpost, and bound in boxes on arm and forehead in prayer.
week.tip: These are Scripture enacted. Asking respectfully about the mezuzah on their door is already a Bible conversation.

week.d: For most Jews an emotional center regardless of their politics — the never-again insurance policy after the Holocaust. Criticism from outsiders lands differently than criticism from inside.
week.tip: Don't lead with your politics in either direction. Ask about family there before you ever offer an opinion.

week.d: Hanukkah (Maccabean rededication — not 'Jewish Christmas'), Purim (Esther, costumes, noise), Sukkot (booths, harvest joy). The year breathes through these.
week.tip: Two fun reversals: the Maccabee story survives in books Christians preserved (1–2 Maccabees), and John 10:22 has Yeshua at the temple for Hanukkah.

aboutyou.t: What 'Christian' has meant to their family
aboutyou.d: Crusader massacres of Rhineland Jewish communities (1096), the blood libel born in Norwich (1144) and repeated for centuries, Easter pogroms, expulsions (England 1290, Spain 1492), forced conversions and disputations, ghettos, Luther's 1543 'On the Jews and Their Lies' — later reprinted by the Nazis — and a Holocaust that grew in baptized Europe's soil.
aboutyou.tip: Carry this history yourself and name it first, unprompted — so they never have to explain it to you.

aboutyou.d: Mainstream Judaism across denominations regards Messianic Judaism as Christianity in Jewish costume — a missionary tactic targeting the vulnerable — and Israel's establishment largely treats Messianic Jews as converts to another religion.
aboutyou.tip: Don't open by litigating the label. Be ruthlessly transparent about what you believe and what you're hoping for; hidden agendas confirm the charge.

aboutyou.d: Organized evangelism of Jews reads as the old coercion by softer means; 'Jews for Jesus' is, for many, a byword for bait-and-switch. The word 'mission' itself carries freight.
aboutyou.tip: Never disguise the invitation. A 'no agenda' Bible study that turns out to have one validates every fear for a decade.

aboutyou.d: American Jewry's deepest anxiety is disappearance by assimilation — every child lost to another faith is subtraction from a people that six million were already taken from.
aboutyou.tip: Honor Jewish continuity concretely: support their kids' Jewish education, celebrate the holidays with them, never frame Jewishness as something to leave.

aboutyou.d: Christians say it as kinship; many Jews hear their living tradition absorbed as a prologue to someone else's religion — flattened into a hyphen.
aboutyou.tip: Say 'Jewish and Christian' and let the real differences stand. Respect reads as respect only when difference is allowed to exist.

aboutyou.d: Supersessionism — the church replacing Israel — is the theological root system under most of the history above. Paul warned the first Gentile generation against exactly this arrogance (Romans 11:17-24), and Romans 1:16 keeps the gospel 'to the Jew first.'
aboutyou.tip: Be able to say plainly, and mean it: 'God has not rejected his people' (Rom 11:1). If your theology can't say that, fix the theology before the friendship.

aboutyou.t: They assume you've never read Torah
aboutyou.d: Most Christians they've met know less Tanakh than a bar mitzvah kid — quoting Isaiah 53 without ever having read Leviticus. The assumption is usually correct.
aboutyou.tip: Read Torah seriously — even follow the weekly parashah. A Christian who knows Vayikra changes the entire conversation.

aboutyou.t: You're asking for more than a belief change
aboutyou.d: For your friend, saying yes to Yeshua risks family, community, identity, possibly a cemetery plot — some families still sit shiva. It is experienced as betrayal of a persecuted people, not as a private opinion swap.
aboutyou.tip: Never minimize the cost — Yeshua didn't (Luke 14:26-33). Offer belonging alongside the argument, and patience measured in years.

aboutyou.t: The memory is in living tissue, not textbooks
aboutyou.d: The stories above aren't ancient history to them — they're grandparents' accounts, a family tree with burned branches. Your friendly invitation arrives inside that inheritance whether you intend it or not.
aboutyou.tip: You are one page in a very long story between your faith and their family. Act like it: slow, honest, and there next year.

doctrine.theirs: Absolute, indivisible unity — Maimonides' second principle. God is one in a way that admits no persons, parts, or incarnation; for a Jew, compromising this is the definition of avodah zarah.
doctrine.bible: The same Shema, affirmed — Yeshua quotes Deut 6:4 verbatim as the greatest commandment (Mark 12:29). The claim is tri-unity within the one YHWH — whose Word, Spirit, and Presence already act as God in the Tanakh and Targums (Memra, Shekhinah) — never three gods.

doctrine.theirs: A human king of David's line who gathers the exiles, rebuilds the Temple, brings world peace and universal knowledge of God (Rambam, Hilchot Melachim 11). Accomplish the list or you are not he — no second chances, no second comings.
doctrine.bible: The same résumé in two acts: first the lowly, pierced, rejected figure (Zech 9:9; 12:10; Isa 53), then the reigning Son of David (Isa 9:6-7; Dan 7:13-14). The rabbis' own ben Joseph/ben David doctrine concedes the texts demand both portraits.

doctrine.theirs: Repentance, prayer, and charity stand in for sacrifice (Hos 14:2; Yohanan ben Zakkai in Avot d'Rabbi Natan 4: deeds of lovingkindness atone); the day of Yom Kippur itself atones for those who repent.
doctrine.bible: Lev 17:11 makes blood God's stated means of atonement, and the Torah never records its repeal. Isaiah 53:10 presents a final asham — a willing guilt offering — after which the new covenant's verdict is 'their sin I will remember no more' (Jer 31:34).

doctrine.theirs: Genuinely varied: olam haba, resurrection of the dead (Rambam's thirteenth principle, the Amidah's second blessing), Gehinnom as mostly a temporary purgation (traditionally capped near twelve months), and broad modern agnosticism about all of it.
doctrine.bible: Resurrection and final judgment (Dan 12:2), eternal life through the Messiah, new creation. More continuity here than either side assumes — resurrection is a shared inheritance, not a Christian invention.

doctrine.theirs: The Sinai covenant is eternal; the 613 commandments bind Jews forever; the Oral Torah is Sinai's authorized interpretation. Any 'new covenant' that loosens Torah self-refutes.
doctrine.bible: Torah is holy and unrevoked — 'I did not come to abolish' (Matt 5:17). Jeremiah's new covenant writes Torah on hearts rather than erasing it (31:33), and Acts 15 brings Gentiles in as Gentiles without converting them into Jews — Isaiah's nations streaming to Zion, not Sinai repealed.

doctrine.theirs: Israel's chosenness is irrevocable — am segulah, covenant people forever. Christian supersessionism is the oldest and deadliest move against them.
doctrine.bible: Unqualified agreement, and non-negotiable for the Christian side: 'the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable' (Rom 11:29); 'has God rejected his people? By no means!' (11:1). The church is grafted into Israel's olive tree — it never replaces it. No replacementism, full stop.

doctrine.theirs: Every person has a yetzer hara and yetzer hatov — an evil and a good inclination — and teshuvah is always available, directly, no mediator required. No original sin; the soul arrives pure.
doctrine.bible: Teshuvah is affirmed and commanded (Ezek 18:30-32) — but the Tanakh's own diagnosis runs darker: 'every intent of the thoughts of his heart only evil continually' (Gen 6:5), 'the heart is deceitful above all things' (Jer 17:9), 'there is no one righteous' (Eccl 7:20). The question is never whether God forgives, but on what basis a holy God does.

doctrine.theirs: Israel personified — the servant is explicitly named Israel (Isa 41:8; 44:1; 49:3), and chapter 53 is the astonished nations confessing what they did to the Jewish people in exile. Rashi, Ibn Ezra, and Radak all read it nationally.
doctrine.bible: Within the Servant Songs the servant is also distinguished from Israel — commissioned to bring Jacob back (49:5-6), innocent of violence and deceit (53:9), stricken 'for the transgression of my people' (53:8). Targum Jonathan calls him Messiah; Sanhedrin 98b names Messiah from 53:4. Both readings are Jewish; only one explains every line.

doctrine.theirs: Jeremiah 31 promises a renewed Sinai in the messianic age — Torah internalized, Israel regathered, everyone knowing God. Nothing in the chapter about a new mediator or a dying Messiah; and the world's condition proves it hasn't arrived.
doctrine.bible: 'Not like the covenant I made with their fathers' (31:32) — new in kind, not merely refreshed — and made with Israel and Judah first. Covenants are cut in blood (Ex 24:8); a Jewish Messiah at a Passover table announcing 'the new covenant in my blood' is quoting Jeremiah and Exodus at once. The universal-knowledge clause awaits act two.

doctrine.theirs: Core doctrine — 'who revives the dead' stands in the Amidah's second blessing, and bodily resurrection at the end of days is Rambam's thirteenth principle. But it is collective and eschatological, not one man mid-history.
doctrine.bible: The same hope (Dan 12:2; Isa 26:19), with one claim added: it began early, in one man, as firstfruits — a debate the NT conducts entirely inside Jewish categories, with Paul splitting the Sanhedrin along the Pharisee/Sadducee resurrection line (Acts 23:6).

doctrine.topic: Worship of a man (avodah zarah / shituf)
doctrine.theirs: Worshiping a human being is the cardinal sin — one of the three a Jew must die rather than commit. Some authorities permit Gentiles 'shituf' (association of another with God); for a Jew, never. This is the bright line under every other objection.
doctrine.bible: Agreement on the standard — the dispute is identity, not the seriousness of idolatry. If Yeshua is YHWH's own arm revealed (Isa 53:1), the one YHWH calls 'me... whom they have pierced' (Zech 12:10), then worshiping him keeps the Shema rather than breaking it. If he is not, the objection stands. Everything hangs on who he is.

suffering-servant.t: Isaiah 53 is our chapter, and you're reading it out of context. Go back to Isaiah 41: 'You, Israel, my servant.' The servant is named Israel again and again — 44, 45, 48, 49. Chapter 53 is the kings of the nations, stunned in the last days, confessing what they did to the Jewish people in exile. Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Radak — that's the Jewish reading.

You're right that the servant is named Israel in those passages — I won't pretend otherwise. But inside the Servant Songs the servant also has a mission TO Israel: 49:5-6 says he's formed from the womb to bring Jacob back and raise up the tribes. Can Israel restore Israel? And in 53:8 the speaker says he was stricken 'for the transgression of my people' — if the speakers are the nations' kings, since when do Gentile kings call Israel 'my people'?

The righteous remnant suffers for the guilty nation — a servant within the servant. And be honest about your history: the national reading became standard partly because Christians turned this chapter into a weapon. Rashi wrote while Crusaders were butchering the communities of the Rhineland.

Then let me say it before you have to: Christians quoted Isaiah while killing Jews, and Rashi's move was partly self-defense — I believe that, and the shame of it belongs to my house. But the messianic reading is older than the church's crimes. Targum Jonathan opens the passage 'Behold, my servant the Messiah.' Sanhedrin 98b derives Messiah's name from 53:4. That reading is Jewish property; the crimes don't erase it.

The Targum gives the Messiah the victory and leaves the suffering to Israel — it's not your crucified Messiah. And 53:10 says the servant will 'see offspring and prolong days.' Your Jesus died childless at thirty-three. The verse disqualifies him on its face.

The Targum reroutes the pain, yes — which itself tells you the plain text made messianic readers flinch. Now stay in 53:10: the same verse says his soul is made an asham — a guilt offering — and THEN he sees offspring and prolongs days. A guilt offering dies; that's what an asham is. A figure whose life is a completed guilt offering and who afterward prolongs his days is either a contradiction — or a resurrection. Read the chapter cold with me, no commentaries on either side, and tell me who you see.

messianic-prophecy.t: The Tanakh gives a checklist. Messiah rebuilds the Temple (Ezekiel 37), gathers the exiles (Isaiah 43), brings world peace (Isaiah 2:4 — swords into plowshares), and fills the earth with the knowledge of God (Isaiah 11:9). Jesus went zero for four. That's not interpretation; that's arithmetic.

I affirm every item on that list — it's the reigning-king portrait and it stands. But the same prophets drew a second portrait: a king who arrives 'lowly, riding on a donkey' (Zech 9:9), one who is pierced and mourned like an only son (Zech 12:10), a servant despised, rejected, cut off from the land of the living (Isa 53). Your own tradition felt the collision so hard it split the Messiah in two — ben Joseph, who dies, before ben David, who reigns.
Ben Joseph is late aggadah, not Torah — a minor figure to absorb a few awkward verses. And 'he'll do the rest at a second coming' is an unfalsifiable IOU. Anyone who failed can promise a round two.

It would be unfalsifiable — except round one is checkable. A ruler from Bethlehem of Judah 'whose origins are from of old' (Micah 5:2). The donkey-king hailed in Jerusalem (Zech 9:9). And a timestamp: Daniel 9:26's anointed one cut off before the city and sanctuary are destroyed — before 70 CE. The IOU has a date and a signature. A deferred second act only matters because the first act happened on schedule.

Every one of those is contested and you know it. Bethlehem Ephrathah may name the clan, not the birthplace; Zechariah's pierced one may be a fallen warrior in the Gog war; Daniel's anointed one is Agrippa or the priesthood in our commentators, Onias or Antiochus-era figures in the academy.

Contested — conceded, every one, and I won't sell you certainty I don't have. So my only ask is this: don't take my reading or Rashi's on authority. They're your books. Put the two portraits side by side — the pierced one and the enthroned one — and ask which figure in history has any serious claim on the first portrait while the whole world, yours and mine, still waits on the second. That's the question; the rest is commentary.

daniel-timeline.t: Daniel 9? The Talmud itself says 'blasted be the bones of those who calculate the end' (Sanhedrin 97b). Generations of date-setters wrecked communities with that chapter. And our commentators read the 'anointed one cut off' as Agrippa, or the anointed priesthood ending at the destruction — not your Messiah.

I'm not calculating an end — that curse can stand. I'm reading a boundary the text already drew: 9:26 says an anointed one is cut off, and AFTER that, 'the people of the prince who is to come shall destroy the city and the sanctuary.' Whatever the seventy weeks mean precisely, that verse puts a mashiach dying before 70 CE. Not my math — Daniel's sequence.

Mashiach there just means 'an anointed one' — every king and high priest was anointed. The academy reads the chapter around Onias III and the Antiochus crisis. You're capitalizing a common noun and calling it Jesus.

Granted — 'anointed' is a broad word, and I'll hold the identification loosely. But set that verse next to your own tradition's memory. Yoma 39b: for the last forty years before the destruction, the lot for the LORD stopped coming up in the right hand and the crimson thread stopped turning white. Count back from 70. On the Talmud's own telling, Yom Kippur's signs went dark starting around 30 CE.

Aggadah is not a lab report. The same page says the Temple doors swung open by themselves. You can't dismiss the Oral Torah all year and then wave one folio as forensic evidence when it points your way.

That's a fair hit, and I'll take it: not proof — your tradition's own memory that something changed in that generation, held loosely. But now stack the loose pieces. Daniel: an anointed one cut off before the destruction. Genesis 49:10: the scepter stays with Judah 'until Shiloh comes' — which Targum Onkelos renders 'until the Messiah comes, to whom the kingdom belongs.' Yoma 39b: forty dark years from about 30 CE. If the window the texts draw is behind us, then the honest question stops being whether Messiah came. It becomes: who came?

temple-atonement.t: This 'no temple, no atonement' argument misreads us completely. Hosea 14: 'Take words with you and return to the LORD... we will offer the bulls of our lips.' When the Temple fell, Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai stood in the ruins and said we have an atonement as effective: deeds of lovingkindness. Teshuvah, tefillah, tzedakah. We never needed blood the way you need us to have needed it.

Ben Zakkai's answer was pastoral genius in a catastrophe, and I honor it — Yavneh saved your people's ability to survive the ruins. But notice what it is: an answer the Torah itself is never recorded giving. Leviticus 17:11 is God's own stated mechanism — 'the life of the flesh is in the blood, and I have given it to you on the altar to make atonement for your souls.' Where does the Torah say that mechanism was provisional, waiting to be swapped out?

The prophets say it constantly. 'I desire mercy, not sacrifice' (Hosea 6:6). 'You do not delight in sacrifice... the sacrifices of God are a broken and contrite heart' (Psalm 51). Samuel: obedience is better than sacrifice. God always wanted the heart. The altar was scaffolding.

Read Psalm 51 one verse further: 'THEN you will delight in right sacrifices, and bulls will be offered on your altar.' David's broken heart doesn't replace the offering — it makes the offering honest. The prophets attack sacrifice without repentance; not one of them repeals Yom Kippur. And if repentance alone had always sufficed, the Day of Atonement was redundant the day it was given.

So your alternative is what — human sacrifice? The Torah calls that an abomination; we don't even eat blood, let alone atone by a man's execution. Nothing could be less Jewish than what you're proposing.

The Torah abominates a life SEIZED — Molech's fire, a victim with no say. Isaiah 53:10 describes the opposite: a servant whose own soul is set as an asham, a guilt offering, who 'poured out his soul to death' willingly and 'bore the sin of many.' Offered, not taken. Your calendar still aches once a year for atonement it has no altar to carry. My claim is that inside the window Daniel drew, that ache was answered — one final Yom Kippur — which is exactly why Jeremiah's new covenant can end, 'I will remember their sin no more.'

new-covenant.t: Read all of Jeremiah 31, not just your verse. The new covenant is with 'the house of Israel and the house of Judah' — not a church. It's Torah written on hearts — the same Torah, kept at last, not replaced. And it describes a world where no one needs to say 'know the LORD' because everyone knows him. Look out the window. Has your covenant produced that world?

I agree with nearly all of that — including the indictment at the end. It names Israel and Judah first, and it's Torah internalized, not Torah abolished; any Christian reading that erases Israel from Israel's own promise has failed before it starts. Where we part: 31:32 says this covenant is 'NOT like the covenant I made with their fathers... my covenant which they broke.' Not-like means new in kind — not Sinai refreshed.
New in kind how? Show me the mediator in the chapter. Show me a dying Messiah, a cross, a Eucharist. They're not there. You're importing your ending into our book and calling it exegesis.

The chapter itself ends on the hinge: 'I will forgive their iniquity, and their sin I will remember no more' (31:34). Forgiveness that final carries a mechanism question — the same Leviticus 17:11 question we keep circling. And covenants in the Tanakh are cut in blood; Sinai's was — 'behold the blood of the covenant' (Exodus 24:8). So when a Jewish teacher at a Passover table lifts the cup and says 'this is the blood of the new covenant,' he's quoting Jeremiah and Exodus in one breath — to Jews, about the covenant promised to Jews. That's not an import; that's an address.

And twenty centuries later the earth is still not full of the knowledge of the LORD. So at best you're holding a deposit slip and calling it the deposit. Why should I accept a covenant that visibly hasn't done what its own text promises?

'Deposit' is exactly the word I'd choose — the forgiveness now, the universal knowledge when the King finishes the reigning portrait. You're waiting for both acts to arrive together; I'm claiming the first is behind us and staking everything on the second. That's the entire disagreement — and notice where we're having it: inside Jeremiah, verse by verse. That's the only place I want to have it.

rabbinic-objections.t: Before you quote a single verse, be honest about what you're asking me. The last time the church wanted Jewish souls it came with disputations we were forced to attend and stakes for the losers. My grandmother's town in Poland had a church at one end and a pit at the other. And now you'd like to study Tanakh with me?

Then let me say it before you have to, and without softening: the Rhineland massacres of 1096 were carried out under a cross. The blood libel was invented in Christian England. Spain expelled your people in 1492 with clergy applauding. Luther's 1543 tract reads like a pogrom manual and the Nazis reprinted it. The Holocaust grew in baptized Europe's soil. I don't ask you to forget or forgive any of it on my schedule. I ask a different question: is Yeshua of Nazareth — a Torah-keeping Jew who never met Christendom — guilty of what was done wearing his name?
'By their fruits you will know them' — your own teacher's test. Twenty centuries of this fruit. At some point the tree is answerable.

And the same teacher said many will cry 'Lord, Lord' and hear 'I never knew you; depart from me, you workers of lawlessness.' I won't defend Christendom, and I'm not recruiting you into its history. The claim I care about predates every crime you named: a first-century claim made by Jews, to Jews, from your scriptures, in your land, before there was a Christendom to sin. Judge that claim by Moses and the Prophets — the very test your tradition would demand.

Even granting all that — Maimonides ruled a Jew must die rather than worship a man. This is not a book-club disagreement for me. It's avodah zarah, the one line with no exceptions, the line my ancestors died rather than cross.

I respect that line more than you might expect — the Shema is not negotiable, and if Yeshua is merely a man, then Rambam is right and I'm the idolater; I accept those stakes. Which means the real question between us can't be settled by my church or your posek — only in the text we share. Zechariah 12:10, YHWH speaking: 'they will look on ME, whom they have pierced, and mourn for him as one mourns an only son.' Start there with me. Not with my history, and not with my institutions — with your prophet.

nt-jewishness.t: The New Testament is a Greek book written for Gentiles that curses my people. 'His blood be on us and on our children' — that one sentence armed a thousand pogroms. Don't stand there and tell me it's a Jewish book.

That verse was wielded exactly as you say, for centuries, and the church that wielded it will answer to God for every pogrom it blessed — I won't dilute that. But open Matthew cold. It begins 'the book of the toledot of Yeshua the Messiah, son of David, son of Abraham' — a genealogy formula straight out of Genesis. Nearly every author is a Jew. And every fight inside it is an intra-Jewish fight — Sabbath halakhah, purity, temple, resurrection — Pharisee-Sadducee territory, not Greek philosophy.

The gospels, maybe. Paul is the problem. He abolished the Torah, invented a religion for Gentiles that Jesus of Nazareth never taught, and you people dress it back up in a tallit and market it to us as Judaism.

The same Paul wrote 'Has God rejected his people? By no means! I myself am an Israelite' (Romans 11:1), warned Gentiles never to boast over the branches, took a vow and paid for temple sacrifices in Acts 21, and circumcised Timothy. The Gentile question was settled at a Jerusalem council (Acts 15) that reasoned from Amos 9 like a beit din: the nations come in AS nations — which is Isaiah's own vision of Gentiles streaming to Israel's God. That's Jewish universalism doing what the prophets said it would, not a new religion.

Then explain the churches. If the book is so Jewish, why has every church I've ever walked past scrubbed the Torah, forgotten Israel, and hung up a blond Jesus? Two thousand years of readers didn't notice what you claim is on every page?

They didn't notice — and that amnesia is close to the church's original sin. Romans 11 warned the very first Gentile generation against it, and they did it anyway, and my tradition is still repenting of it. Which is why my invitation runs opposite to the old one. Not 'leave your people and enter my church' — but read Matthew with me as what it actually is, a Jewish book making a Jewish claim, and hold me accountable to your text every single time my religion forgot it.
